description: We're a team of curious, ambitious problem-solvers passionate about space exploration, aerospace engineering, scientific research, and technology. We enjoy tackling complex problems, exploring unconventional ideas, and turning scientific data into meaningful, practical solutions.
summary:
As humanity prepares to live on the Moon and Mars, understanding combustion beyond Earth is essential. That's why we created Ember Atlas, an interactive dashboard that transforms NASA's microgravity combustion research into an accessible scientific exploration experience.
Using experimental records from five main NASA investigations, we developed a dashboard featuring a physics-inspired flame simulator, interactive scientific graphs, evidence-based fire safety insights, and a research network that reveals connections and gaps in available experimental data.
Users can explore how gravity, oxygen, pressure, airflow, and materials relate to combustion behavior, compare ISS-like and lunar-habitat environments, and investigate how space research connects to wildfire science, cleaner combustion, and fire safety on Earth.
It is built using React, Python, PostgreSQL, scientific visualization tools, and machine learning research, Ember Atlas connects complex datasets with meaningful scientific exploration.
We're making NASA's combustion research easier to explore, understand, and apply because the future of living beyond Earth depends on understanding the environments we're entering.
details:
Imagine trying to understand how fire behaves in a place where flames don't rise, smoke doesn't disperse normally, and the atmosphere is completely different from Earth's. As humanity prepares to establish habitats on the Moon and eventually Mars, understanding combustion in these environments becomes increasingly important.

That's the problem we wanted to explore with the challenge, Flame in Freefall, powered by our interactive scientific dashboard, Ember Atlas.

NASA has already conducted extensive combustion research in microgravity. However, the findings are spread across experiments, datasets, technical papers, and individual measurements. We wanted to transform this valuable research into something interactive, understandable, and useful for exploring future space-habitat fire safety.

What We Built

Ember Atlas brings together research from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository, focusing on five major combustion investigations: FLEX, CFI, SAME-R, SPICE, and BASS-II. Together, they cover liquid-fuel flame extinction, cool flames, smoke aerosols, soot formation, and solid-material combustion.

Our platform combines this research into four interconnected experiences.

Scenario Simulator: Users can explore different combustion environments, including ISS-like and lunar-habitat scenarios, by adjusting gravity, oxygen concentration, atmospheric pressure, airflow, and material. A physics-inspired flame animation responds to these changes, while interactive scientific graphs help users explore relevant experimental measurements. We also calculate important quantities such as oxygen partial pressure. For example, our ISS reference atmosphere has approximately 21.28 kPa of oxygen partial pressure, compared with 19.22 kPa in our lunar-habitat reference scenario. This demonstrates why oxygen concentration alone cannot determine combustion conditions.

Fire Safety Insights: We wanted to go beyond showing scientific data and explain why it matters. This feature connects environmental conditions and materials with relevant combustion research, helping users investigate possible hazards and understand the evidence supporting each observation.

Cinematic Evidence Graph and Research Gap Explorer: Our interactive research network visualizes relationships between experiments, materials, parameters, and scientific evidence. The Research Gap Explorer uses a color-coded heatmap to identify parameter combinations with abundant, limited, or no matching records in our indexed dataset. This makes research coverage easier to understand without implying that every missing combination has never been investigated.

Earth Applications: Space research can also help us understand challenges on Earth. We created interactive educational demonstrations connecting combustion science to building-material fire safety, cleaner burners, wildfire behavior, soot and air pollution, and engine efficiency.

How We Built It

We developed Ember Atlas using React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS for the interface; Python and FastAPI for scientific processing and backend services; and PostgreSQL for organizing research records and experimental parameters. We used Plotly for scientific visualizations and Cytoscape.js for our interactive evidence network. We also incorporated AI-assisted scientific research processing and developed a ridge regression machine learning model using NASA FLEX burning-rate measurements. The model was evaluated using grouped cross-validation and mean absolute error. Its numerical predictions remain separate from the public simulator's measured evidence.

A major technical challenge was making research from different investigations comparable without misrepresenting it. We considered differences in experimental conditions, units, incomplete parameter information, repeated records, and the distinction between measured data and visual simulations.

Why Our Approach Is Different

We didn't want to create just another animated flame simulation or a static collection of NASA research papers. We wanted to connect the two by allowing users to explore combustion conditions, examine real experimental evidence, visualize relationships between studies, identify limitations in available research coverage, and understand possible applications. Our goal is to make advanced combustion research accessible to students, researchers, engineers, and anyone curious about the future of space exploration.

We believe that before humanity can safely build homes beyond Earth, we must better understand one of the most fundamental forces we live with: fire.
